name: Browns Restaurant
description: Browns occupies 131-133 George Street, a pair of category B-listed townhouses built between 1780 and 1790 as part of the New Town's original George Street terrace, with alterations carried out by the architect John Bryce in 1883. The building has a genuinely distinguished architectural pedigree: William Burn kept his office at No.131 from 1822, and after 1844 the celebrated Scottish architect David Bryce - designer of Fettes College and the Royal Infirmary - worked from the same address. No.133 later passed through very different uses, including a spell as the Leicester Permanent Building Society's offices and, more recently, a hairdressers, before its current life as part of Browns' brasserie.
interesting_fact: No.133's most notable resident predates all of that commercial history: the portrait painter Sir Henry Raeburn, whose likenesses of Sir Walter Scott and the skating Reverend Robert Walker rank among Scotland's best-known images, lived there for a time, as did the novelist and illustrator Catherine Sinclair. Raeburn's own studio still stands nearby on York Place - easy to imagine him passing this same George Street frontage, now filled with Browns' pavement tables, on his way between the two.
